utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is case number IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Prosecutor, would you like to introduce your team to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution is represented by Michael Blaxill, Sureta Chana, and myself, Franck Terrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will now turn to Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm appearing without a team; it's just a one-man show this afternoon. Attorney Nick Kostic appearing for General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Good afternoon to everybody, and of course to General Galic. Before beginning our work this afternoon, I would like to tell you that the Trial Chamber is not sitting in a full bench because Judge Riad is busy with another case in the Appeals Chamber, which you may already know. I suggest the following: This Chamber, without Judge Riad, could hear the parties today and subsequently render a decision. I would like to know whether there are any objections from either of the parties. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For the Defence, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to take up the matter of the question that you've just asked, which deals with the ability to proceed without Judge Riad. I have another problem concerning proceeding today which I want to address. You were kind enough, the Chamber was -- I filed a motion at one point and asked for a continuance of the provisional release hearing because I had just begun a trip to Bosnia about, I think, a day before I received the notice, and then proceeded to go to Bosnia and return to the States later, towards the end of May. Unfortunately, and I can't tell you why and it's something that I have actually taken up with the Registry, the decision which you rendered in regard to your decision on my motion seeking postponement, although it's dated May 17th, and I have no doubt that that's when it was rendered, that was never forwarded to my office. The way I obtained it was to obtain it from a member of the Prosecution today when I -- I arrived here the day before today. I've taken that up because it's somewhat bothersome that I wouldn't have received it. I also did not receive -- the reason I'm here, of course, is because back on April 11th, when we had a Status Conference, I think verbally you indicated you wanted to have a Status Conference on today's date, which was good, and I put it in my calendar. So I'm here pursuant to that verbal notice from you and was only informed about this potential hearing on this date. The reason I raise that issue is that while I was in Republika Srpska, I took some steps and efforts to investigate and deal with the issue of the motion that I filed. As you know, there are other cases not -- well, I'm not sure if it's before this Trial Chamber, but it certainly is before some other Trial Chambers, to deal with the issue of release and there have been some decisions made. I took some efforts to see if I could get an input from the particular authorities in Republika Srpska who would deal with the Tribunal and who would be able to provide the Tribunal with information -- well, the Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber with information in regard to this particular motion. The problem is that being unaware that we would proceeded today, that I was not able or did not have time to secure their presence. Judging from -- and being informed in Srpska by the officer who is the liaison officer with the Tribunal, Mr. Jovicic, I was informed that he played certainly a role in these kinds of hearings. This has to do with commitments by Republika Srpska; this has to do with commitments by the Ministry of Justice. He works under the Ministry of Justice, in that entity. That is the problem in regard to this issue on today's date. So I wanted to indicate that to you, and, quite frankly, I'm not sure why I'm not receiving the documents. I did receive finally yesterday your document dealing with the Prosecutor's motion to extend time, but that was only received in my office, I think, on the day before yesterday. So I'm trying to clear that issue up. That is one of the problems that I have today. The other issue that I wanted to talk to the Tribunal or the Chamber with is this: whether the Court or the Chamber, in lieu of oral testimony, would be just as happy to receive affidavits submitted to the Court in regard to these issues. Obviously, if not, I would have to then get the witness here to testify. I'm looking for some guidance in that regard. I know that in one of the other cases in front of the other Trial Chamber, the lawyer made an offer of proof, in other words, informed the Trial Chamber himself of the background of the situation, the reasons why he feels there ought to be a release. It also would represent what the witness or witnesses would testify to or what the defendant could give in terms of information. So that is another way of doing it. That is the issue, Judge, that I have on today's date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, in relation to the composition of the Chamber without Judge Riad's being here, do you have any objection to the Chamber hearing your comments and then taking a decision, or what is your position, before we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Judge, I know that Judge Riad is in an important matter, and I have no objection to proceeding without him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Registrar, do you have any information about the reasons why counsel did not receive the documents in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, unfortunately, I have no answer to give you. I think that we might need a five-minute break so I can get some information from the Registry, that is, to learn whether the motion was sent to Mr. Kostic by fax, which is what is usually done, and try to conduct a little investigation to see what happened in respect of that notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We're going to see if we can do that at some point, because perhaps we should take a break and find out. I believe that we have here at least two questions, preliminary questions: The first has to do with timeliness of the evidence in support of the motion, and the other is a point which affects the first, which is a specific detail. In any case, I might give the floor to the Prosecutor so that he can tell us. But before anything else, it seems to me that a motion requesting provisional release is an urgent request, in my opinion, and a very serious one at that; urgent and therefore must be the subject of an immediate decision. And the Chamber has set a date for this hearing and, at the request of the Defence, postponed it. It's serious, because I believe that the arguments and allegations must, in some way, be already proved. We cannot make a motion -- present a motion and then look for support of the arguments in the motion. However, as I've already said, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecutor so that he can react to the issue raised by Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll try to give you our point of view, but I would like to point out that at this point of our deliberations, I really don't understand the request Mr. Kostic is making. Is he asking that the Chamber issue a postponement for this very urgent issue, urgent, as you've said, or is he in a position today to give us the nature of the evidence which he plans to submit to the Tribunal in support of the motion? I don't know for sure, but what I would simply like to say is that, in principle, these hearings are not evidentiary hearings, responsible for gathering evidence in support of the motion or against the motion. Ordinarily, the documents are disclosed to the Tribunal, and then the Tribunal confirms the allegations -- or rather, which confirm the allegations that are contained in the motion. And in support of the motion, in theory, I see no problems with documents being submitted by Mr. Kostic in support of his request. However, hearing the witnesses during this type of hearing seems to me to be very difficult to organise and even to conceive of. From our point of view -- and I'm reacting perhaps without thinking too much about what I'm saying -- my first thought is to say that I agree for the documents, and possibly even affidavits, subject of course to our knowing what the writer of these affidavits has to say. Would these be official documents? Are the documents of an official character? Are they indicating the commitment on the part of a recognised authority or is this a private person? All of this will be reviewed. In any case, a document, we agree. A witness, well, my position is more nuanced. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, would you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would intend to do is, in regard to any witnesses who -- for example, an affidavit from my client, anybody who has knowledge or had knowledge of his whereabouts and his activities for the relevant period of time, that could be done in affidavit fashion. Obviously the documents from the officer in charge of the liaison for Srpska, which would -- I think there would be two types of documents; one -- they would both be official documents, because one is an official document of the entity in a form of a guarantee; the other document would be in a form of a letter from the officer in charge, which would indicate that they are prepared, and I of course would suggest -- I will suggest or would suggest to the Court certain conditions -- if there is a release, certain conditions that would have to be met, and that would be outlined again in an official document, a condition such as a ban on travel, depositing whatever passport or travel documents, and the place of residence, things of that nature. So those would be the types of documents that I would provide to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, if I have understood you correctly, you are not in a position to discuss your motion with the Chamber today, or are you in a position to discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can do today is to give you a background and give you an oral presentation as to some of these issues, but I cannot supply you with either evidence or documents from the Republika Srpska entity. That is not quite available yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, the Defence should supply all justifications in support of a request for provisional release at the time that the request is made and not after two months. That's really the issue. If, Mr. Kostic, one looks at the motion which you've submitted, one should be able to say that there isn't a sufficient basis and that it should not be granted. However, since this is an important issue, that is, provisional release of an accused, the Chamber nonetheless expected to discuss this at this time. But now you're telling us that you're not in a position to do so, and I'm going to make a proposal. I can't do the Defence's work, but I think that it might be more reasonable to postpone this hearing yet once again so that you can be in a position to come to argue your motion. Or there's another possibility that we can discuss as well. You said that you are not in a position to prove the allegations, and if we discuss things as they stand now, you might not have your motion granted. Therefore, what is it that you're asking the Chamber? Ultimately, that is the question that Mr. Terrier asked. What is the purpose of your motion? Where does it stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would ask for, and I think what would make most sense in order to do this motion just once, I would like the opportunity to do everything at one time, which would be to submit all of the written documents, affidavits, and then also make an oral presentation which, of course, would be much shorter, and we could take care of it at one time. That is what I would -- I would prefer it, of course, if I could. I don't think it would in any way affect the working of the Chamber. And I think the other thing is that by submitting these documents ahead of time to the Prosecution, they would have an ability to review them and comment on them. In other words, I wouldn't be just handing them to them the morning of or minutes before the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the most reasonable thing to do would be to reason the way you have, and to take a decision, I've got to consult my colleague Judge Wald. All right. I'm going to ask you to excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a break, because the Chamber would like to have a response to the question about what happened with the documents that were not sent to Mr. Kostic in due time. And after the break, we'll take a decision. In any case, before we take our break, I would like to tell the parties that for today we had planned to discuss the request for provisional release, but there were other issues having to do with the pre-trial management of the case. So we'll take a break, and after that we'll come back to take decisions on the question of provisional release, and then we'll continue with the pre-trial management of the case itself. I would ask Diana, our registrar, to get us some information about the question raised by Mr. Kostic. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Diana, have we received an explanation, and if so, would you give it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Registry apologises for the delay that it caused to this hearing. The explanation of the Registry is as follows: The ordinary procedure has us fax all decisions rendered by the Chambers on the very day that they are rendered, except when the Registry knows that the counsel in question will be in The Hague for his work or to see his client. In that case, the Registry is responsible for the trip of the counsel, and considering that Mr. Kostic came to The Hague from the 23rd to the 25th of May, 2000 -- therefore the Registry realising Mr. Kostic was going to The Hague on those dates, they did not fax that decision to Mr. Kostic, put it into his mailbox. We looked in that mail box and we found the decision there. Therefore it has been in his mailbox ever since the 17th of May. Unfortunately, that mailbox was not checked for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give these documents to Mr. Kostic these documents now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I will take it down to reception to give you all of the documents that we found in his mailbox today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why it took you so long?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had to first see if we could -- find out whether the documents had been faxed, and then we realised Mr. Kostic had come on the 23rd of May to The Hague, and so we put the documents in his mailbox and we had to investigate things on that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for your explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order in question is at the very top of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to take notice of the fact that the order really was signed on that day and was really registered on that date. Mr. Kostic, now you've got all the decisions, and the Chamber will grant to you 15 days to support your request with the documents that you consider necessary. Therefore, the Chamber, instead of not granting the motion, will give you that extra time. We're going to do that in writing, and the Prosecutor will have the time to make a statement about the documents, and the Chamber will take its decision following that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy pointed out to me that we're giving a time period to Mr. Kostic to submit to the Chamber the documents in support of his motion, the Prosecutor will have the opportunity to respond, and the Chamber, after that, without needing another hearing, will render its decision. We will now move on, Mr. Kostic, and you should know that all this time that we're wasting here is very expensive for the International Community, and so one must be careful to be sure that this does not happen again. Now let me move to a discussion with the parties about the pre-trial status of the case. As you know, the last conference was held on the 11th of April, 2000, and we now have to review the progress made in the preparation of the case. The following issues will be discussed now, at least three points we have to deal with: the disclosure of documents in accordance with Article 66(A)(ii) of the Rules; the second point will be the preparations of the Defence; and thirdly, the submission by the Prosecutor of exhibits mentioned in 65 ter of the Rules. We are going to check the objective sought by that Rule. First point, the disclosure of material by the Prosecutor. Since the last Status Conference, we were able to see that the Prosecutor has finalised the disclosure to the Defence the documents mentioned in Rule 66(A)(i). The Chamber granted the Prosecutor an extension of time, until today, to disclose the documents mentioned in 66(A)(ii) in B/C/S. Mr. Terrier, could you please tell us whether all these documents have been disclosed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the totality of those documents are here at the disposal of Mr. Kostic, who would like us to mail them to him rather than taking them with him. But in any event, we are meeting the decisions of the Chamber. I simply wish to say, as you referred to 66(A)(i), that the document I mentioned to the Tribunal are files regarding the mortars and raids of Sarajevo, and snipers that shelled Sarajevo, but they include also other types of documents which we are, strictly speaking, not obliged to disclose but we are disclosing nevertheless, and they are reports on the part of investigators, experts, regarding these snipers and shelling, and all these documents, in any event, are at the disposal of Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The Prosecutor has said -- I'm not sure. Have you had any communication with the Prosecutor? Can you confirm what the Prosecutor has just said, that they have been disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have to understand that I do not know all of the information and all of the documents that the Prosecution has. I only know what they have given me. Pursuant to, I believe, your order on the 11th of April, on May 12th to 13th -- I'm not sure of the date -- I did receive seven binders which were identified with certain types of witnesses, and essentially they were called -- one binder was "shelling witnesses," another binder was called "expert witnesses," another binder was "UNMO witnesses," another one was "UNPROFOR witnesses" another was called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, excuse me for interrupting you. You will have an opportunity of reviewing all those documents. Perhaps this is not quite the time to tell us which documents are contained in the binders. The Prosecutor has told you that he will send you or make available to you all those documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I received the documents I've indicated to you. There was one other group called "international civil affairs witnesses"; those documents, once they arrived in my office, the Prosecutor indicated that they were sent to me in error. So without looking at them, I sent them back, so I don't know what is contained in those documents. Those documents I do not have, as of today's date. They are not in my possession. They -- pursuant to their request, were sent to them. So those are the documents I have. I'm also told that the Prosecution will be sending me additional documents, fourteen binders available today, and that sometime in the next -- and I don't have an approximation as to the time, but I will be receiving approximately another 80.000 pages of discovery materials in regard to this case, but obviously arrangements have to be made to receive those 80.000 pages of discovery. That is what has been told to me by the Prosecution, and that's what I know, and I've told you the amount of discovery that I received as of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you any comments to make, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm sorry that these 14 binders which we are communicating to Mr. Kostic contain a large number of pages, not quite 80.000, but it is an important case and I think that Mr. Kostic must study those documents as quickly as possible so that we can proceed normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Terrier, that is what I'm concerned about; that is, that we must get on with the case and end the pre-trial stage. I must go on to the second item, that is, the preparations of the Defence. I draw attention, first of all, of Mr. Kostic to the fact that the Chamber had to reject a preliminary motion regarding defects in form of the indictment because it was submitted more than two months after the deadline. However, the Chamber has noted that in another motion regarding the documents required, the Defence relied on rules of procedure that are inapplicable before this Tribunal. And the motion for provisional release of General Galic is a good example, as I have just said. It is an urgent motion, and a very important one, a serious one, and we are where we are today since the motion was filed. So I would like Mr. Kostic to explain why this is so. As I have told you, we have many things to do, we have a lot of work to do, and I would like to have an explanation why you filed all these motions which question the procedures applied by the Tribunal without respecting the time limits; in other words, they were not filed in a timely fashion. Can you explain that to us, Mr. Kostic, why this is so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed this same issue at the April 11th meeting, and I have your decisions on the motions. It only deals, really, with one motion that I think the Court felt was untimely. The other motions that were filed were just rejected for the reasons indicated, and at that point my work began to work on the building of the defence. So all I can tell you is that my work is in that direction. I suspect that with the discovery materials that I'm going to be receiving, I'm going to be using up all of the hours that are available to me in order to prepare both the defence, but also to review what is being given to me. As you know, the Registry has limited our time that we can work on any one case; they've cut back by 50 hours per month. So I will do the best I can and I will move ahead with that, but you have to realise, on the basis of what has been told to you this afternoon, that I have an absolute mountain of information that I have to go through, and only I can review that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, Mr. Kostic, so that things should be quite clear, the Chamber must know the position of General Galic. General Galic, would you please stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any observations to make with regard to the preparation of your defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I find it difficult to give you a definitive answer because, as far as I can see, these materials are still arriving, so that a large number of those documents are not available to me, or are only available in English so I cannot follow. I expected to receive today some materials, as was indicated. Regarding my defence, I said last time that the appointment, the temporary appointment, which is still in force, affects the organisation of the Defence and its work, and I think an attorney should be designated who will be a permanent Defence counsel. Whether that will be Mr. Kostic or someone else, for the moment, I still favour Mr. Kostic as a choice. I can see that something is wrong but I'm not sufficiently legally educated to know what it is that is causing an obstacle. That would be my answer in brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now going to go on to the third point, the disclosure of documents by the Prosecutor, not 65 ter of the Rules but a certain outlook regarding the future. You know that some documents mentioned in Rule 66 will be disclosed today, so we thereby have reached a new stage in the proceedings. Therefore, I would like to hear the views of the parties, beginning with the Prosecutor, as to whether he can inform us regarding the status of the preparations in line with Rule 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure, Rule 65 ter (E), and specifically whether the parties have had a chance to meet to discuss the pre-trial proceedings. Where do we stand in relation to the pre-trial stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the situation is as follows: We are communicating today, within the frameworks given by the Chamber, the documents in English and in Serbo-Croatian so that General Galic can himself take part in his defence. A few days ago we sent to Mr. Kostic a fax reminding him of the rulings of the Chamber and asking him to set a date for a possible meeting so that we might review the indictment and the charges it contains, and also examine what would be accepted as proven, of which judicial notice could be taken, and what will be challenged. We will not be able to organise that meeting next week, but before the end of the month, if that is possible and if Mr. Kostic is agreeable. After that first stage, we would like -- and those are questions that we put to Mr. Kostic -- we would like to meet with General Galic himself. Of course, General Galic is quite free to agree or not to answer our questions. But we would like to make such a request for a meeting with General Galic. After that we would be, we hope, in a position, within the deadline set by the Chamber, that is, the 10th of July, to communicate a pre-trial brief. That is where we stand at present. A question that I would like to raise may be a secondary one but it has to do with translation. In another case before your Chamber, we were told that we would have to submit our motions, requests, and briefs in English and French simultaneously. I'm quite in favour of this but I'm asking whether it might be possible to give the Prosecution, and of course the Defence, additional time for the translation to be completed, because the Chamber knows that we do not have our own translation services and we're not managing to deal with this translation problem. If we have a 50-page document of a pre-trial brief, it would require about two weeks for translation, and if we need to have it translated, as instructed by the Chamber, this would delay matters. So that is my concern. Perhaps the Chamber would agree, in this sort of transitional period, when these rules are not fully established, that we might give a certain extended time for the other language, if we could have additional time for the translation into the other language. That would be a matter I should like to put before you. We are at the disposal of Mr. Kostic for a meeting, we would like to meet General Galic, if he wants to meet us, and we will be able, by the 10th of July, in one of the languages of the Tribunal -- I may add, it will probably be in English -- to submit our pre-trial brief and all the other documents envisaged by Rule 65 ter (E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, what are your comments regarding this forecast of the pre-trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I'm troubled by it because of the information that I received in terms of the amount of discovery that I'm going to be receiving. It is, in my opinion, absolutely impossible to do that with the amount of the discovery materials that I will be receiving. I can't see how it can be done on the basis of the new rules of the Registry. I'm being very honest with you because I am trying to determine, in my own mind, the amount of time that one needs to read and analyse the documents which will be forthcoming. It isn't just a matter of reading a document, it's a matter of analysing it and seeing how it fits into the case. So I'm troubled by it, and if I was to give you a forecast, it would not be a very good forecast because I don't think I have all the information needed to give you such a forecast. I don't know, for example, whether any of the discovery raises any additional issues, whether any of the discovery points the nature of the defence in one area or another, and things of that nature; I am also not sure in terms of the expert testimony which is coming, what will cause that to the Defence in terms of having to respond, research, and do those things. So I find that I'm troubled by it, and I think it will be very difficult. I always do like to meet with counsel and discuss the issues and cases and all of that, but unfortunately, at this point, I don't know, let's say, in two or three weeks, if I work on the case which I will, whether I still would be in a position, with all of the materials that are coming in, to be able to tell the Prosecutor, "Yes, I agree with you; we don't have a problem on this fact," or not, because I just don't -- I don't know what's there, is what I'm trying to tell you. So I have some doubts whether it can be done that quickly. That's my response, at least in terms of one of the comments by the Prosecutor. As far as the meeting with General Galic, I think that will not occur now. He is not in a position to do that at the present time. I think he wants to go through the materials, he wants to discuss the matter with me, and then that decision will be made down the road, whether he does or does not want to meet with the Prosecutor. I hope I've answered, I think, the three questions you had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kostic. Perhaps, this is a suggestion I would like to make, it would be a good idea to have a meeting with the Prosecutor at least to discuss the quantity of documents so that you can have some guidelines. I think it would be useful. I'm not saying to the Prosecutor that this issue should be discussed, I'm just saying that it would be useful, perhaps, to have a first glance at the indictment, which is a public document -- it has been in existence for a long time -- to see if there are things that General Galic can accept straight away and others that he will never accept, and a whole series of other minor matters which could have considerable repercussions even in the preparatory work of the Defence. So I'm just leaving this suggestion with you, with the parties. I think that the first step, to work effectively and efficiently, would perhaps be to meet; that is what I think, but of course I can't impose it on you. There is another aspect to this matter. The Prosecutor, Mr. Terrier, mentioned the date of the 10th of July, and it is true that we set that date. But that date had before it the dates of the 30th of May, the 1st of June, the 5th of June, and the 8th of June, and due to various preliminary motions and this motion for provisional release, it was not possible and it is not useful to have that Pre-Trial Conference then. I'm talking as the Pre-Trial Judge now, and I think that this pre-trial brief should be at the end of the preparatory stage and not at the beginning. Perhaps we need to review the whole calendar for the pre-trial stage, because I do wish to give the parties an opportunity to meet and discuss matters and then to come to a Status Conference with the Pre-Trial Judge to see what are the results of those discussions. One might put aside straight away things, stipulations, between the parties, they don't need any additional work; then we can review the issues that are contested and see whether any agreement can be reached on them; and once we have heard each other and discussed these matters, only then could we go on to the actual physical compilation of this brief. That is my understanding of these proceedings. Rather than having a pre-trial brief and then discussing it, it is preferable to reverse the order: to discuss things first, see what the agreements and disagreements are, and after that we will have all that in a file. I think that is the best way to prepare a trial. In my opinion, having a good pre-trial stage is a guarantee for a good trial, which means if we start badly in the pre-trial stage, it will be very difficult to do well during the trial itself. But of course this requires a certain amount of time, because, as I have said, the Chamber does want to conclude the pre-trial stage as soon as possible, that is to say, to be ready to start the trial. Even if we cannot start it as we have planned -- I'm saying this in connection with the question raised by Mr. Terrier at the last Status Conference -- we need to be ready for the trial itself, to begin the trial, and then we will see which Chamber will be trying the case, this Chamber or another one. But we can't begin if we're not ready. So we have to complete the pre-trial stage in order to be able to begin as soon as possible. Therefore, I think that perhaps the first step, as I have already said, and I apologise for repeating myself, would be for the parties to meet, to talk, to see what the stones are and then deal with them, what the issues are and then address them. I think that for the moment there is nothing more, at least not on my agenda. But in any case I can open the floor to either of the parties if they have anything to add. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would take the liberty of making a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, suggestions are always welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently, in this case file, the Defence is having some trouble getting started, and so we're trying to set a date for the next Status Conference, during which a report will be given to the Trial Chamber about what's been accomplished by both of the parties, by the Prosecution and the Defence, in order to reach a sort of agreement, or in any case, an observation as to what is in agreement and what is not in respect of facts that are in the indictment. I think we should have this time period, because if we don't have this time period, I think it's going to be very difficult to move forward. What I would like today is, at the end of this meeting, for you to set a date for the period during which the Status Conference will be held in which we have to report on what has been done in respect of the relationships between the parties and the preparation of this case. I'm not talking about a hearing to discuss provisional release but rather the continuation of the preparations for this trial. I think it would be good for us to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand, I think, the position of the Prosecutor, having been one, by the way, earlier in my career. This office has investigated this particular matter, this case, since 1994, so they've had six years to work on the case. They've collected information, they've interviewed witnesses. They know the case, I would imagine, extremely well. It's a good team, it's a large team, and they're ready and prepared to go. The problem is that I'm not in the same position as they are. I've not had six years, I've not had two years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, we are already familiar with those arguments. As a member of the Bureau, and I've received all that information, so we can go more directly to the question of the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I'm very glad you're familiar with that argument, because I think it's important in this case. What I have now is what's been outlined. It has not been controverted by the Prosecution in terms of the materials which will be receiving. I mean that's obvious, so there's an awful lot of work to be done. Remember, there's two things to do: one is to go through the discovery materials, and the other is to put together a defence. They're connected but different work. Your question is: Do I have any problems in sitting down with Mr. Terrier and discussing the issues of the case? The answer is no. I'm willing do that and will continue dealing with him. But the problem, of course, is I have to sit down with him, being informed, knowing the issues in the case, knowing the law in the case, and quite frankly knowing how I'm going to defend any particular issue or aspect or count in the case. So in the beginning, our conversations are not going to be as useful because I'm still learning and going through the discovery materials, but they will pick up. Bottom line is I would be happy to meet with Mr. Terrier. There may be some facts and issues which are very straightforward. If they are, I don't have a problem. And I will continue doing that. There's not a problem in regard to doing that; I tell you that clearly. However, again, you know what my concern is, and I've said it and I'm not going to repeat, and that has to do with the mountain of materials that I have. Finally, I would think that we will need some amount of time to come back to you and meet with a Status Conference. I have some thoughts along that line; I'm sure Mr. Terrier does. Whether you care to hear it at some point, I would be happy to give you some idea. But again, I will continue working and dealing with the Prosecution on some of these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kostic, we hope that that cooperation will continue. I have a question. Are you in a position, before you leave The Hague, to meet with Mr. Terrier for a first reading of the indictment? The indictment; I'm speaking only about the indictment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think I would have some time before I leave, although I am leaving tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. Is it possible to think that by three weeks from now, we could have a Status Conference in order to see where we stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't think -- I think it would not be helpful. I do not think that I will be able to go through everything that is coming my way in terms of the discovery materials. I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say the date already mentioned, the 10th of July. This was already mentioned, that is, a month from now, the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: If you want me here on the 10th of July to tell you how I'm doing, I'd be very happy to come; I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that Mr. Kostic would make all efforts possible to go through the documents. Perhaps I should not be the one to suggest that to you, but you've got many documents and I think that some of them could be left with General Galic already so that he can move things forward instead of sending everything to the United States; to Mr. Kostic, rather. It's not for me to say to you what you should do. Still, I'm trying to be practical. I'm trying to be practical. We are here in order to do practical things. I believe that having said this, we have dealt with all the issues. Just to summarise the most important things, I would say that Mr. Kostic -- well, we've said 15 days, that is, the 23rd of June. I believe it's a Friday. By that time, you're going to file the documents necessary in support of the request for the motion for provisional release. On the 10th of July, we are going to meet again for a Status Conference, at least in order to take the first look at where we stand and possibly to programme the subsequent conferences, because as I've said, I would like to programme things from the point of view of having the parties here so that they can work together. If Mr. Kostic is in the United States and Mr. Terrier is here, it of course is difficult to work together. Therefore, you have to come to The Hague and stay here to work in order to prepare the case properly. I think that that is the most important thing that comes from this conference today in terms of compromise and commitments. I have only now the responsibility of giving the floor to General Galic. General Galic, would you rise please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you whether you have any specific comments having to do with your detention conditions or your health.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, last time, on the 11th of April, I reported about my medical condition. It hasn't changed significantly since then. My problems with my leg persist, but I hope -- and in fact I've been told that it will take a whole year for the leg to be restored back to normal. I also have some minor medical problems, but I have no complaints regarding treatment. The conditions in detention are such that I have no objections to make. Thank you once again. I made my comment last time about the television. We do have a satellite programme now, so we can watch Croatian television and Pink [phoen], but we do not have the programme of our state, the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it would be nice if we could follow those programmes as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we have any other matters to deal with, and so I adjourn the session, and we will see one another again on the 10th of July to speak together about the preparations for this case. Good evening.
